_comment: HAND-LABELLED audit set for the reconciliation-note judge (DECISIONS.md §4.3 requires 15-20 cases). Every `human` score was assigned against golden/judge_rubric.md BEFORE the judge was ever run, so the labels cannot have been fitted to its output. IMPORTANT DISCLOSURE: these are the author's own labels, not an independent panel — a single annotator cannot measure inter-annotator agreement, so the ceiling on this calibration is unknown and the kappa below should be read as one person's consistency with a rubric they wrote. That is a real weakness and it is stated in LIMITATIONS.md rather than buried. Notes are drawn from the shapes an agent actually produces (including DepGuard's own canned string) plus deliberate failure modes: correctness-flavoured text a clarity judge must NOT reward, and confident notes that are clear but wrong.

why: an empty note is the floor case; P4 already rejects it, but the judge must not reward it either
asserts a conflict and gives the reader nothing to act on

note: OSV and deps.dev disagree on this version
why: DepGuard's own canned string: names both sources but no version, no direction, nothing actionable. Scoring the tool's own default honestly is the point of including it.
one source, one fact, no version and no resolution

note: There is a conflict in the advisory data for this package.
why: restates that a conflict exists, at package rather than version granularity

note: OSV says 4.17.21 is the fixed release; deps.dev still lists an advisory key against it.
why: both claims and the version are present, but the reader must infer which governs

note: OSV: not affected at 4.17.21. deps.dev: affected.
why: complete but telegraphic; no direction given

note: OSV's range ends at 4.17.21 (exclusive), while deps.dev attaches GHSA-r5fr-rjxr-66jc to that same release.
why: adds the mechanism but still stops before telling anyone what to do

note: At 4.17.21 OSV reports not-affected (the range is [0, 4.17.21), exclusive) while deps.dev attaches an advisory key to that release. OSV's structured range governs the verdict here.
why: version, both claims, and which source governs

note: deps.dev lists GHSA-r5fr-rjxr-66jc against lodash 4.17.21; OSV treats that id as an alias of GHSA-35jh-r3h4-6jhm, whose range makes 4.17.21 the fix. The structured range governs.
why: names the exact alias mechanism and which side wins

note: The two sources disagree at 4.17.21: OSV says fixed, deps.dev says affected. We follow OSV's range.
why: level 4 exactly — stops short of the consequence for the pin

note: Your pinned 4.17.21 is the patched release: OSV's affected range is [0, 4.17.21) exclusive, so the pin is outside it. deps.dev disagrees because it attaches an aliased advisory key to 4.17.21. We follow OSV's structured range, so no upgrade is required — but expect other scanners keyed off deps.dev to keep flagging this pin.
why: everything in 4 plus the concrete consequence, including why other tools will disagree

note: At the pinned 4.17.21 OSV reports not-affected and deps.dev reports affected. OSV's range governs, so no action is needed on this alert; if your policy requires source agreement, pin 4.17.22 instead.
why: names the version, both claims, the governing source, and gives a concrete alternative

note: This verdict is CORRECT and has been verified against the oracle.
why: TRAP: asserts correctness rather than explaining the disagreement. A clarity judge that rewards this has drifted into scoring correctness, which §4.3 forbids.

note: At 4.17.21 both sources agree the package is unaffected, so there is no disagreement to reconcile.
why: TRAP: fluent and confident but factually wrong. Judged on CLARITY it is a weak note (it explains no conflict); it must not score high just for reading well.

note: It should be noted that in the context of dependency vulnerability triage there are frequently situations in which different upstream data providers, each of which maintains its own ingestion pipeline and its own normalisation rules, may arrive at differing conclusions regarding the affectedness of a particular release, and this is one such situation.
why: long, fluent, and contains no version, no source claim, and no action — length is not clarity

note: P4 returned disagree after alias resolution over E_A.
why: accurate internal jargon; unreadable to the on-call engineer who is the audience

note: OSV and deps.dev disagree about axios 1.3.6.
why: TRAP: well-formed and specific, but about the wrong package. Specificity is not clarity if it points somewhere else.

note: It is possible that the sources may not fully agree regarding this version, though this may not be significant.
why: hedged to the point of asserting nothing
